title: Eating before, during and after training
summary: The daily food basics for a tennis player, what to eat and drink before, during and after training, points just for teenagers, and the rule on caffeine and supplements.

sections.h: Why is food part of training?
p: Tennis and gym training use a lot of energy. Your body gets most of that energy from carbohydrate: bread, rice, potatoes, pasta, beans and lentils, fruit and dates.
Getting stronger happens between sessions, and your body needs enough protein and energy to repair and build muscle. A teenager also needs energy for growing, on top of training.

Most of what a player needs comes from normal home food. Sports nutrition guidelines, including the recent one for tennis, say "food first". This lesson isn't a personal diet. For a personal plan, talk to a sports dietitian.
sections.callout: Food is part of training. With enough food, your body trains better and recovers better.

p: These basics matter more than the details before and after training:
list: Regular meals: three main meals, plus one or two snacks on heavy training days. Don't skip breakfast.
Carbohydrate at every meal: bread, rice, potatoes, pasta, lentils or beans, and fruit. On heavy training days, give these a bigger share of your plate.
Protein at every meal, not just dinner: for example a palm-sized piece of chicken, meat or fish, two or three eggs, or a bowl of lentil soup with bread and yoghurt.
Fruit and vegetables every day and at most meals: salad, fresh herbs, tomato, cucumber and whatever fruit is in season.
Water through the day. The details are in the lesson "Water, sweat and playing in the heat".
sections.callout: A simple plate for each meal: one part bread, rice or potatoes, one part protein, and vegetables or fruit.

sections.h: Teenagers: calcium, vitamin D and iron
p: Teenage athletes are more likely to run low on calcium, vitamin D and iron. The best way is to get these from food:
list: Calcium for bones: milk, yoghurt, a yoghurt drink like ayran or kefir, and cheese, every day and across several meals.
Vitamin D: your body makes a big part of it from sunlight on your skin, and it's also in foods like eggs and fish.
Iron: red meat, chicken, fish, lentils and beans. Teenage girls lose more iron because of their periods.

Better iron absorption: eat fresh fruit or vegetables with your meal. Tea can lower iron absorption, so drink it between meals, not with them. This matters most when your meals are low in meat, chicken, fish, fruit and vegetables.
sections.callout: I don't recommend any pills, powders or supplements here. If a doctor prescribes something like iron or vitamin D after a blood test, that's the doctor's call.

p: The goal is to start with enough energy and a settled stomach. A little carbohydrate before long or hard sessions helps performance, though that finding comes mostly from endurance sport, not tennis. For short sessions it may not make much difference.
list: 2 to 4 hours before: a normal meal with carbohydrate, some protein, and not too fatty or heavy. For example rice and chicken, pasta, or bread with eggs and cheese.

30 to 60 minutes before, if you're hungry or your last meal was a while ago: a small, light snack like a banana, a few dates, some raisins or a piece of bread. These two time windows are the course's own working rule, not a study result.
Early morning training: if there's no time for a full meal, at least have a light snack and a glass of water.
Water: drink with your meal and keep sipping until you start.
Very fatty, fried or spicy food right before training can sit heavy on your stomach.
sections.callout: Try any food routine on training days first. Match day isn't the time to try something new.

p: For most sessions water is enough. Have a few sips in each break. How much and when is in the lesson "Water, sweat and playing in the heat".
In sessions longer than about an hour and a half, or in the heat, a little carbohydrate and salt helps too:
list: Carbohydrate: every few breaks, a few bites of banana, one or two dates or some raisins. In total, at least about one banana per hour.

Amount: one banana has about 25 g of carbohydrate, which is the low end. The tennis guideline for adults says 30 to 60 g an hour in sessions of 90 minutes to 3 hours, so if you still run flat, add a few dates. For growing players there's no set number. Ask a sports dietitian.

Salt, if you sweat a lot: a little salty snack like pretzels or bread and cheese in the breaks, and after training a salty yoghurt drink like ayran or some salty food. This is practical advice, not a study result. If a doctor has told you to limit salt, follow that.
Eat something your stomach is used to and that you've tried before.
sections.callout: In a long session, eat a little at a time from the first hour. Don't wait until you're already worn out.

p: Within about 1 to 2 hours after training, have a meal or snack with carbohydrate and protein, plus water. This helps refill your energy and repair muscle.
If you train or play again within about 8 hours, don't push this meal back. If the gap is longer, what you eat across the whole day matters more than the exact timing.
list: Rice, or rice with lentils, with chicken and salad
Bread with eggs or cheese, and a piece of fruit
A glass of milk with a banana or a few dates
Yoghurt with bread or fruit
After a lot of sweating: a glass of salty yoghurt drink like ayran with your meal
sections.callout: After training: carbohydrate, protein and water, within 1 to 2 hours.

sections.h: Two sessions in one day: gym and tennis
p: Tennis and a gym session on the same day is fine. The order of the day and the gap between sessions are in the lesson "Training around tennis and matches". This part is only about food and water in between.
list: After the first session: water, and a snack or meal with carbohydrate and some protein.

Gap under about 2 hours: small, light snacks you know well, like a banana, dates, bread and cheese or a glass of milk, a little at a time and often. This 2-hour mark is the course's own working rule, not a study result.
If both sessions are hard and the gap is under about 8 hours: your body needs more carbohydrate, so eat those small snacks several times in the gap.
Longer gap: a normal meal that isn't too heavy, like rice and chicken, and a small snack close to the second session if you need it.
On hot days, also replace the water and salt you've lost between the two sessions.
sections.callout: On a two-session day, get the food and water for in between ready in advance.

sections.h: Teenagers: eat enough for growing and training
p: A teenager who trains needs energy for both training and growing. A weight-loss diet without a doctor's advice isn't right for a growing player.
When the body gets less food than training and growth need for a long time, researchers call it "low energy availability". In girls and boys alike, it can hurt health and performance.
This lesson can't tell you what's causing a problem. Only a doctor can. These signs (a list from the course itself, not from one study) mean it's time to see a doctor:
list: Tiredness that lasts for weeks and doesn't get better with normal sleep and rest
Periods that have stopped or become irregular
Losing weight when you weren't trying to
A lot of worry about food, weight or body shape
sections.warn: Long-lasting tiredness, periods that stop or become irregular, or weight loss: talk to a doctor. These signs have different causes and only a doctor can tell what's going on.
sections.callout: Parents: talk about the player's energy, strength and how they feel, not their weight or body shape.

p: Under 18: no caffeine to play better, so no coffee or tea for that reason, and no energy drinks. Paediatric experts say caffeine and the stimulants in energy drinks have no place in what children and teenagers eat and drink. Keeping coffee and tea out for this purpose too is the course's own caution.

Adults: if you're used to tea or coffee and it suits you, a normal cup about an hour before playing may help a little. The studies used bigger doses, about 3 mg per kg of body weight, which is around 200 mg for a 70 kg player. Not in the late afternoon or evening, because it can mess up your sleep.
At any age: your programme doesn't need any pills, powders or other supplements. Some supplements can harm your health or contain banned substances.
sections.callout: Under 18: no caffeine for playing, and no energy drinks. At any age: food, not pills and powders.
